SOCIAL STUDIES
NATIONAL VALUES EDUCATION

PRIMARY 1
PRIMARY 2

TOPIC - MEANING OF SOCIAL STUDIES
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning of Social Studies
3. How Man Solved His Problems
4. Lesson Evaluation and Weekly Assessment (Test)
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, most of the pupils should have attained the following objectives -
1. explain the meaning of social studies.
2. state the problems of man.
3. state how man solved his problems.
LEARNING BEHAVIOURS
The pupils can identify and describe their environment.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of chart showing different things in our environment.
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
Scheme of Work

Course Book
All Relevant Material
Online Information

- First Term Workbook - Weekly Assessment Book for Social Studies (Primary 1)
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
LESSON 1 - INTRODUCTION
1. Social studies is the study of man and his environment.
There are different kind of people in our environment.
Man’s environment includes other people, animals, houses, schools, hospitals, banks, cars, trees, rivers, mountains, etc.
2. Social studies is also the study of man and how he lives with one another.
There are a lot of people in our environment.
These people speak different languages like Yoruba, Hausa, Igbo, and so on.
They learn the language and traditions (cultures) of other people in his environment.
People in our environment also include - our father, mother, brothers and sisters, uncles and auntie, neighbours, etc.
3. Social studies is the study of how man and how his problems are solved in the environment.
There are other things in our environment such as animals (domestic and wild), plants, rivers, mountains, etc.
Some of these things are problems to man.
For example,
- how to plant crops,
- protect himself from the wild animals,
- how to move from one place to another,
- how to protect himself from the thief, etc.
LESSON 2 - HOW MAN SOLVED IS HIS PROBLEMS
The problems of man are solved in many ways such as,
1. Trial and error
2. The use of technology
3. Education
4. Continuous training
1. TRIAL AND ERROR
Man has tried many things to solved his problems.
In these ways, he failed, succeed, discovered and developed a lot of things to solve his problems.
2. THE USE OF TECHNOLOGY
Man developed technology such as hoe and cutlass, tractor, fishing net, motor, etc. to solve his problems.
3. EDUCATION
Man trained the young ones on how to identify problems and apply appropriate tools to solve them.
4. CONTINUOUS TRAINING
Man continue to train himself to be able to use the new and appropriate tools to solve his problems.
For example, the use of tractor instead of hoe and cutlass.
LESSON 3 - REVISION AND WEEKLY ASSESSMENT BOOK
First Term Workbook - Weekly Assessment Book for Social Studies (Primary 1)
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
1. To introduce the lesson, the teacher revises the previous lesson. Based on this, he/she asks the pupils some questions.
2. Teacher organizes pupils in groups or pairs depending on the size of the class and available instructional materials.
3. Teacher displays chart showing some of the problems of man such as in family, movement, etc.
4. Teacher lets pupils identify and describe how man solve his problems.
Pupil’s Activities - Learners identify and describe how man solve his problems.
5. Teacher listens to the pupils and uses their relevant responses to introduce the lesson.
Pupil’s Activities - Learners pay attention to the lesson introduction to understand its concept.
6. Teacher uses the chart to leads a discussion on the meaning of social studies.
Pupil’s Activities - Learners explain the meaning of social studies.
7. Teacher guides pupils on how man solve his problems in the environment.
Pupil’s Activities - Learners identify and analyze how man has solved his problems in the environment.
8. Teacher summarizes the lesson on the board using appropriate lesson evaluation.
Pupil’s Activities - Learners participate actively in the summary of the lesson by responding correctly to questions and write as instructed.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
LESSON 1 - INTRODUCTION
MEANING OF A FAMILY
Family is made up of father, mother and their children.
A family is made of other people who are related to one another by blood.
This family is called extended family.
MEMBERS OF THE FAMILY
The members of family are as follows:
1. Father
2. Mother
3. Children
4. Uncles
5. Aunts
6. Cousins
7. Nephews
8. Niece
9. Grandparent
10. Inlaw
LESSON 2 - MEMBERS OF THE FAMILY
1. FATHER
Father is the male parent of the family.
2. MOTHER
Mother is the female parent of the family.
3. CHILDREN
Children are the dependant ages of the family.
4. UNCLES
Uncle is the brother of one’s father or mother.
5. AUNTS
Aunt is the sister of one’s father or mother.
6. COUSINS
Cousin are the children of one’s uncle or aunt.
7. NEPHEWS
Nephew is the son of one’s brother, sister, brother-in-law or sister-in-law.
8. NIECES
Niece is the daughter of one’s brother, sister, brother-in-law or sister-in-law.
9. GRANDPARENTS
Grandparent is the parent of one’s father or mother.
They are also called grandfather or grandmother.
10. IN LAWS
In law is the relationship by marriage.
LESSON 3 - REVISION AND WEEKLY ASSESSMENT (TEST)
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
1. To introduce the lesson, the teacher revises the previous lesson. Based on this, he/she asks the pupils some questions;
2. Teacher organizes pupils in groups or pairs depending on the size of the class and available instructional materials.
3. Teacher displays chart showing father, mother and their children.
4. Teacher lets pupils as groups or pairs to identify the father, mother and their children.
5. Teacher asks pupils few questions about their father and mother for academic purposes. For example, occupations.
Pupil’s Activities - Learners appreciate the importance of their parents and other members of the family.
6. Teacher uses the chart and pupil’s relevant responses to introduce the lesson.
Pupil’s Activities - Learners pay attention to the lesson introduction to understand the concept of the lesson.
7. Teacher leads a discussion on the meaning of family.
Pupil’s Activities - Learners explain the meaning of family.
8. Teacher uses another chart to introduce members to the family.
9. Teacher guides pupils to identify members of their family.
Pupil’s Activities - Learners identify and appreciate the members of their family.
10. Teacher summarizes the lessons on the board using appropriate lesson evaluation.
Pupil’s Activities - Learners participate actively in the summary of the lessons by responding correctly to the questions and write as instructed.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.

LESSON 1 - INTRODUCTION
Family is made up of father, mother and their children.
This family is also known as nuclear family.
Other types of family is known as extended family.
There are 2 types of family,
1. Nuclear family
2. Extended family
QUALITIES OF A GOOD FAMILY
Family has qualities.
The qualities of a good FAMILY are what is expected of each family member such as -
1. Honesty
2. Contentment
3. Discipline
4. Obedience
LESSON 2 - QUALITY OF A GOOD FAMILY
1. HONESTY
Honesty means telling the truth at all time.
That’s, the act of being truthful to one another in all things.
2. CONTENTMENT
Contentment means to be happy with what you have, who you are, and where you are.
That’s, to be happy and satisfied with what you have.
3. DISCIPLINE
Discipline is the way of training people to obey rules regulations.
Sometimes, punishment is used to correct disobedience.
4. OBEDIENCE
Obedience is the willingness to the right things.
Other qualities of a good family are as follows:
5. Support one another as a family.
6. Love and caring for other family members.
7. Ensuring the security their family members.
8. Create sense of belonging.
9. Open communication.
10. Making each member of the family to feel important, valued, respected and esteemed.
11. Showing respect towards one another.
LESSON 3 - REVISION AND WEEKLY ASSESSMENT (TEST)
As stated in learning performance and lesson evaluation.

1. To introduce the lesson, the teacher revises the previous lesson. Based on this, he/she asks the pupils some questions.
2. Teacher organizes pupils in groups or pairs depending on the size of the family and available instructional materials.
3. Teacher asks pupils to state what to do to make their family happy.
Pupil’s Activities - Learners demonstrate how things they do that make their family happy.
4. Teacher listens to the pupils and uses their relevant responses to introduce the lesson.
Pupil’s Activities - Learner pay attention to the lesson introduction to understand the concept of the lessons.
6. Teacher leads a discussion on the qualities of a good family.
Pupil’s Activities - Learners analyze and appreciate the qualities of a good family.
7. Teacher organizes pupils to demonstrate the qualities of a good family.
Pupil’s Activities - Learners play the role of a family by demonstrating the qualities of a good family, e.g. honesty, love, caring, etc.
8. Teacher summarizes the lessons on the board using appropriate lesson evaluation.
Pupil’s Activities - Learners participate actively in the summary of the lesson by responding to questions correctly and write as instructed.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
LESSON 1 - INTRODUCTION
Culture is the ways of life.
It is the general custom, arts and beliefs a particular group of people.
For example - the Yorubas, Hausas and Igbos.
Culture can be passed down from generation to generation.
PEOPLE’S WAYS OF LIFE
1. The way they dress.
2. The way dance.
3. The food they eat.
4. The language they speak.
5. The religion they practice.
6. The work they do.
7. The religious practice.
TYPES OF CULTURE
There are two types of culture -
1. Material Culture
2. Non - Material Culture
LESSON 2 - MATERIAL AND NON MATERIAL CULTURE
MATERIAL CULTURE
Material culture are parts of culture we can make, see, touch and feel.
They are physical objects, resources and space people use to define themselves.
For example,
1. Building
2. Book
3. Plate
4. Tools
5. Food, etc.
NON - CULTURE MATERIAL
Non - material culture are parts of culture that we cannot see but can hear and feel.
They can only be known from what people do.
Examples Non Materials Culture
1. Language
2. Religion
3. Greetings
4. Dancing
5. Dressing
6. Eating habits

INTRODUCTION
Moral is the principle of what is right and wrong in human behaviours.
TYPES OF MORAL

MEANING OF GOOD MORAL

For example - truthful, obedience, respectful, etc.
To make our society safe, we must learn and demonstrate acceptable beliefs and values.
CHART SHORT A POEM ON GOOD AND BAD MORAL

topics.title: Values That Show Bad Morals in Our Society | Primary 1 (Basic 1) First Term Civic Education
topics.content:
CIVIC EDUCATION
PRIMARY 1 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 10
THEME - NATIONAL CONSCIOUSNESS
PREVIOUS LESSON - Public Enlightenment Campaigns - HIV/AIDS Education and Drug Abuse | Primary 1 (Basic 1) First Term Week 9 Civic Education
TOPIC - VALUES THAT SHOW BAD MORALS IN OUR SOCIETY
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning and Examples of Bad Morals
3. Examples of Bad Morals
4. Effects of Bad Morals in the Society
5. Ways of Avoiding Bad Morals
6. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
7. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the simple meaning of bad morals.
2. Mention examples of bad morals.
3. State some effects of bad morals in the society.
4. Mention ways of avoiding bad morals.
5. Explain why good behaviour is important in the society.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about public enlightenment campaigns, HIV/AIDS education and drug abuse.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by teaching pupils behaviours that are wrong and should be avoided in the society.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Pictures showing good and bad behaviours.
2. Charts showing good moral values.
3. Pictures of people telling lies, fighting and stealing.
4. Story cards about good and bad behaviour.
5. Pictures showing people helping one another.
METHODS OF TEACHING
The teacher uses observation, explanation, questioning, identification, demonstration, comparison, repetition and simple practical activities.
Additional methods include discussion, storytelling, picture observation and the use of simple examples from the pupils’ homes, school and community.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Civic Education Textbook for Primary 1
2. Lagos State Scheme of Work for Civic Education
3. Teacher’s Lesson Guide
4. Other Relevant Materials
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Good morals help people live peacefully with one another. Bad morals are behaviours that are wrong and can cause problems at home, in school and in the society.
In this lesson, pupils will learn about values that show bad morals in our society.
MEANING OF BAD MORALS
Bad morals are wrong behaviours that do not show good character.
A person who shows bad morals may behave in ways that hurt others or cause problems in the society.
EXAMPLES OF BAD MORALS
Examples of bad morals include:
1. Lying
2. Stealing
3. Fighting
4. Bullying
5. Cheating
6. Disrespecting elders and other people
7. Destroying public property
8. Refusing to obey rules
9. Taking things that do not belong to us
10. Using insulting words
EFFECTS OF BAD MORALS IN THE SOCIETY
Bad morals can:
1. Cause fighting and disagreement.
2. Make people afraid or unsafe.
3. Make people lose trust in one another.
4. Damage relationships.
5. Lead to destruction of property.
6. Make the community less peaceful.
WAYS OF AVOIDING BAD MORALS
We can avoid bad morals by:
1. Telling the truth.
2. Respecting other people.
3. Obeying rules.
4. Sharing and helping others.
5. Avoiding fighting and bullying.
6. Taking care of public property.
7. Returning things that do not belong to us.
8. Listening to parents, teachers and responsible adults.
9. Saying sorry when we do something wrong.
10. Choosing good friends and good behaviours.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
1. Bad morals are ______ behaviours. A. helpful B. good C. wrong
2. Which of these is a bad moral? A. Sharing B. Lying C. Helping
3. Stealing means taking something that ______ belong to you. A. should B. always C. does not
4. Which of these can cause disagreement? A. Fighting B. Helping C. Sharing
5. A person who bullies others shows ______ behaviour. A. kind B. bad C. helpful
6. We should ______ other people. A. respect B. insult C. hurt
7. We can avoid bad morals by telling the ______. A. story B. lie C. truth
8. Destroying public property is a ______ moral. A. good B. bad C. useful
9. Bad morals can make people lose ______ in one another. A. food B. trust C. books
10. Which of these shows good behaviour? A. Helping others B. Stealing C. Fighting
ANSWER KEY
1. C 2. B 3. C 4. A 5. B
6. A 7. C 8. B 9. C 10. A
SUMMARY
Bad morals are wrong behaviours that show poor character. Examples include lying, stealing, fighting, bullying, cheating and disrespecting others. Bad morals can cause disagreement, fear and loss of trust.
We should avoid bad morals by telling the truth, respecting others, obeying rules, helping people and living peacefully.
PRESENTATION
STEP 1: Introduction
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher asks pupils to mention some good and bad behaviours they have seen at home, in school or in their community.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention examples of good and bad behaviours.
STEP 2: Meaning of Bad Morals
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains that bad morals are wrong behaviours that do not show good character.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and explain bad morals in their own simple words.
STEP 3: Examples of Bad Morals
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher shows pictures of lying, stealing, fighting, bullying and other bad behaviours.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify and name the bad behaviours shown in the pictures.
STEP 4: Effects of Bad Morals
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains how bad morals can cause fighting, fear, disagreement and loss of trust.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention some problems that bad behaviours can cause.
STEP 5: Ways of Avoiding Bad Morals
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains ways of avoiding bad morals, such as telling the truth, respecting others, obeying rules and helping people.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention good behaviours they can practise instead of bad morals.
STEP 6: Practical Activity
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher presents simple situations and asks pupils to identify whether the behaviour is good or bad and what the pupil should do instead.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify the bad behaviour and state the good behaviour that should replace it.
STEP 7: Group Activity
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher divides the pupils into four groups.
- Group 1: Mention four examples of bad morals.
- Group 2: Mention four effects of bad morals.
- Group 3: Mention four ways of avoiding bad morals.
- Group 4: Mention four good behaviours that should replace bad morals.
The teacher guides the groups and allows each group to present its activities/work.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils work in groups, identify, discuss and present their answers to the class.
STEP 8: Lesson Summary and Evaluation
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher summarizes the lesson and asks pupils simple questions about bad morals and how to avoid them.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen to the summary and answer the teacher’s questions.
CONCLUSION
Bad morals are wrong behaviours that can cause problems in the society. Pupils should avoid lying, stealing, fighting, bullying and other bad behaviours. They should practise honesty, respect, kindness, obedience and peaceful living.
NEXT LESSON
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils,
1. What are bad morals?
2. Mention two examples of bad morals.
3. Mention two effects of bad morals.
4. How can you avoid bad morals?
5. Mention two good behaviours you should practise.
